deep.reconstruction:
The page has no calculations. It is a methodological reflection, continuing the previous page's remark that physical facts depend on the choice of axioms (temperature has an absolute zero, time does not).

(1) Analogy. Assuming Newton's law of gravitation and then stating Kepler's first law as a separate law is redundant, because the elliptic orbit follows from the inverse-square law. Modern form (my addition): the inverse-square force gives Binet's equation u'' + u = GM/h^2 with u = 1/r. Its solution r = p/(1 + e cos θ) is a conic.

(2) Heat conduction. The general law is the heat equation u_t = k u_xx; in general dimension, u_t = k Δu. Two simple, often-observed special cases are mentioned:
(a) A rod 0 ≤ x ≤ L with its ends held at temperatures T0 and T1 admits an equilibrium. This is the stationary solution u_s(x) = T0 + (T1 − T0) x / L, with u_s'' = 0.
(b) With the same boundary conditions, every initial temperature distribution tends to the stationary state as t → ∞. In modern terms (my addition): write u = u_s + w. Then w(x,t) = Σ b_n exp(−k n²π² t / L²) sin(nπx/L) → 0, with b_n the Fourier sine coefficients of u(x,0) − u_s.
Hilbert's point: (a) and (b) are purely logical consequences of the conduction law. Treating them as 'obvious' or as separate laws of nature betrays the scientific character of physics.

(3) Consistency of physical axioms. Whoever sets up a general law of nature must check that it is consistent with itself and with the simplest observed facts. In higher dimensions an equilibrium is a solution of Laplace's equation Δu = 0 in a region with prescribed boundary values: the Dirichlet problem. Before C. Neumann and H. A. Schwarz proved that this boundary value problem is solvable, it was not clear that the heat law did not contradict the observed occurrence of temperature equilibria. The same holds for electrostatics. Hence the Neumann–Schwarz existence proof is indispensable for heat theory and is also a physical achievement: it establishes the consistency of the axioms of heat conduction. This anticipates the next page's claim that existence of solutions to boundary value problems and eigenfunction expansions matter to physicists. It is an instance of the programme of Hilbert's 6th problem.

(4) A new paragraph begins. What Gordan and Klein want, to reduce everything to 7 operations, is exactly the aim of Hilbert's axiomatic method. Every correct mathematical fact could then be proved and checked mechanically, and every error detected; the reading 'Erbsen' is uncertain. The page breaks off at 'Nur der Anlass-'.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there are no computations.
Historically, Kepler's first law follows from Newton's law only in the two-body idealisation. Hilbert's 'is a consequence' is the usual simplification.

Calling the Dirichlet-problem existence proof 'Neumann–Schwarz' is somewhat loose. C. Neumann (method of the arithmetic mean, 1870/1877) and Schwarz (alternating method, 1870) gave different proofs for different classes of domains. Neither covers all domains, and later work (Poincaré, Hilbert's own revival of the Dirichlet principle in 1900) was needed for more general ones.

deep.surprise_reason: These are philosophical notes. Hilbert's view that existence proofs for boundary value problems ensure the consistency of physical axioms is known from his lectures on the axiomatisation of physics (Corry) and the 6th problem. The explicit pairing of the Neumann–Schwarz proof with the consistency of heat-conduction axioms, and the Gordan/Klein remark, are nice unpublished details but not new results.
